analysis.one_liner: Strips federal tax breaks from big investors that own 50 or more single-family rental homes.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 12 cosponsors and a Senate Banking Committee hearing, but it never got a committee vote or a floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would deny interest and depreciation deductions to any taxpayer that owns 50 or more single-family rental homes, removing two of the biggest tax breaks large corporate landlords use when they buy up existing houses. The deductions come back only if the owner sells a home to a family to live in or to an affordable-housing nonprofit. Newly built homes and smaller landlords below the 50-property line are exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters and families trying to buy a house. Large investors that own 50+ single-family rentals would lose tax advantages worth billions over time, which raises their cost of outbidding ordinary buyers for existing homes and creates a tax reason to sell homes to owner-occupants or community land trusts. Small landlords with fewer than 50 properties are untouched.

how_it_helps.text: Denies the mortgage-interest deduction to any taxpayer that owns 50 or more single-family rental homes, so large investors lose a major tax subsidy for financing buy-ups of existing housing stock.
Also denies depreciation deductions on those homes, closing a second way large owners shelter rental income.

Restores the interest deduction only in the year a property is sold to an individual for their principal residence or to a qualified nonprofit such as a community land trust or land bank, giving big owners a tax reason to sell homes back to families rather than to other investors.

Leaves small landlords below 50 properties completely alone and exempts newly built housing, so the bill targets investors buying existing homes rather than penalizing construction or mom-and-pop rentals.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporate owners of single-family rental homes — including single-family rental REITs and private-equity-backed landlords — through higher tax bills on their portfolios. Tenants of those specific large landlords could see some of the cost passed through as higher rents if the owners don't sell.

drawbacks.text: The 50-property threshold is a bright line: a firm with 49 homes keeps every deduction, and critics could argue the line rewards staying just under it.

Large owners could respond by raising rents on tenants or selling to other large investors rather than to owner-occupants, which would shrink rental supply in tight markets before adding any new homes.

The construction carve-out is broad: any property built by the taxpayer, or bought before a unit was ever occupied, keeps full deductions — so a large investor that shifts to build-to-rent keeps its tax breaks entirely, blunting the bill's effect on the overall share of homes owned by institutions.

Denying deductions does not cap rents or limit who can buy; it changes incentives, and its real-world effect on home prices depends on how much of large investors' edge actually comes from these tax breaks.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a targeted, not sweeping, affordability measure: it hits only the largest single-family landlords, exempts new construction, and steers sales toward owner-occupants and nonprofits. Its strongest honest criticism is the pass-through risk — tenants of affected landlords could pay more before any homes change hands — plus the build-to-rent carve-out that lets large investors keep deductions by building instead of buying. On balance the design pushes costs onto a concentrated industry rather than the public, but it is an incentive-based approach whose effect on prices would be gradual, not a guarantee of cheaper homes.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Senate Finance Committee for the rest of the two-year Congress — it never got a committee vote, and the Senate never voted on it before the session ended.

narrative.text: Senator Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on July 11, 2023, joined at the start by seven other Democratic senators including Finance Chairman Ron Wyden; it was read twice and referred to the Finance Committee.
Twelve senators total signed on as cosponsors — 11 Democrats and 1 independent; no Republican ever did.

On April 18, 2024, the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee held a hearing at which the bill's subject was taken up, printed as S.Hrg. 118-712 — but the bill itself remained in the Finance Committee, which has jurisdiction over tax law.
No markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever followed, and when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, the bill died there.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporate single-family landlords are better off: they keep the interest and depreciation deductions the bill would have taken away, and their tax-advantaged position when bidding for existing homes is unchanged.

for.name: Sherrod Brown
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-OH), Chair of the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: Elizabeth Warren, John Fetterman, Jeff Merkley, Jack Reed, Tina Smith, Tammy Baldwin, Sheldon Whitehouse and other Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, bringing total support to 12 senators.

against.name: Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, but as chair of the committee where it sat he never scheduled a markup or committee vote, and the bill never advanced past referral.

against.name: Single-family rental industry, including operators represented by the National Rental Home Council
against.role: Industry trade group and corporate landlords
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed restrictions on large investors buying single-family homes while the bill was pending.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or an independent; no Republican signed on, and the bill never reached a vote where the partisan split would have been tested.

industries.industry: Institutional single-family rental landlords (rental REITs and private-equity-backed operators)
industries.note: The bill directly removes interest and depreciation deductions for any owner of 50 or more single-family rentals, raising their tax bill and narrowing the financial edge that lets them outbid families for existing houses. Only a sale to an owner-occupant or affordable-housing nonprofit restores the deduction in the sale year.

Newly built homes are exempt from the deduction denial, so large investors that want institutional-scale returns are pushed toward building new housing rather than buying up existing homes, which adds supply.

industries.industry: Affordable-housing nonprofits, community land trusts, and land banks
industries.note: The bill defines these organizations as qualified buyers whose purchases preserve the seller's deduction, making large landlords likelier to sell to them and putting permanently affordable stock within their reach.

industries.industry: Banks and lenders financing large single-family rental portfolios
industries.note: With interest no longer deductible on portfolios of 50 or more homes, the tax value of heavy borrowing falls, which would modestly reduce demand for acquisition financing from the largest operators.
